Agent: Of course, here are three easy dessert recipes that you might enjoy:

1. Chocolate Peanut Butter Cups
Ingredients:
- 1 cup creamy peanut butter
- ¼ cup powdered sugar
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 1 cup chocolate chips
- 1 tbsp coconut oil

Instructions:
1. In a mixing bowl, combine peanut butter, powdered sugar, and vanilla extract.
2. In a separate bowl, melt the chocolate chips with coconut oil in the microwave or over a double boiler.
3. Grease a muffin tin and fill each cup halfway with the melted chocolate.
4. Add a spoonful of peanut butter mixture to each cup, then top with the remaining chocolate.
5. Refrigerate for at least one hour or until the chocolate is firm.

2. Lemon Bars
Ingredients:
- 1 ½ cups all-purpose flour
- ½ cup powdered sugar
- ¾ cup unsalted butter, softened
- 4 eggs
- 1 ½ cups granulated sugar
- ⅓ cup fresh lemon juice
- 2 tbsp lemon zest
- ¼ cup all-purpose flour
- ¼ tsp salt

Instructions:
1. Preheat the oven to 350°F and grease a 9x13 inch baking dish.
2. In a mixing bowl, combine flour and powdered sugar.
3. Add the softened butter and mix until crumbly.
4. Press the mixture into the prepared baking dish.
5. Bake crust for 18 to 20 minutes, or until golden brown.
6. In a separate mixing bowl, whisk together eggs, granulated sugar, lemon juice, lemon zest, flour, and salt.
7. Pour the mixture over the prepared crust and bake for 18 to 20 minutes, until set.
8. Cool the bars completely, then dust with powdered sugar before serving.

3. Strawberry Shortcake
Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 3 tbsp granulated sugar
- 1 tbsp baking powder
- ½ tsp salt
- 6 tbsp unsalted butter, chilled and cubed
- 1 cup heavy cream
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 2 cups sliced strawberries
- Whipped cream, for topping

Instructions:
1. Preheat oven to 400°F and grease a baking sheet.
2. In a mixing bowl, whisk together flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.
3. Add cubed butter and mix with your fingers until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.
4. Pour in the heavy cream and vanilla extract and mix until a dough forms.
5. Transfer the dough to a floured work surface and knead briefly.
6. Roll the dough into a ¾-inch thick disc.
7. Use a biscuit cutter or a glass to cut out rounds of dough and place them on the prepared baking sheet.
8. Bake for 18 to 20 minutes or until golden brown.
9. Split the shortcakes in half and layer the bottom half with sliced strawberries.
10. Top with whipped cream and the remaining half of the shortcake, and serve.

Enjoy!

The What A Do Theatre of Springfield is known for taking chances. For its first show of the 2017 calendar year, it produces an adaptation of S.E. Hinton’s classic young adult novel “The Outsiders,” which features a cast almost entirely under the age of 18.
At times the performances are rough, like wood sculpture not yet completely hewn, partial shavings curl near the surface, but this roughness fits the show and its world of rumbles and street violence. What this cast may lack in polish, it makes up for in raw energy, youthful vigor, and the artful production values of a professional theatre company to back them.
Though frequently banned for its violence and its portrayal of underage drinking and smoking, Hinton’s 1967 novel “The Outsiders” has been taught in many middle schools across the country and will be well known to many.
The protagonist and narrator Ponyboy Curtis (Nick Wheeler) shows promise academically and is good at writing compositions for English (ostensibly because he is the author), but this promise is threatened by the violence of his town as “Greasers” are locked in an unending battle with the “Socials,” which is basically a class conflict.
The conflict escalates when Johnny (Hunter King), Ponyboy, and Two-bit (Darius Walker) are seen with the presumed girlfriends of two socials Cherry (Averi Beck) and Marcia (Maddy Heywood).
The conflict between the two gangs builds to a final rumble that will settle scores once and for all, but not before head social Randy Adderson (Nyle Rosenbaum) tries to make peace. In the end, Ponyboy gets his chance to make something of himself.
The final message of this coming-of-age story is that there is escape from the gang violence of the street and that people have names, hopes and dreams and not just labels like “Greaser” or “Social.” Both are messages that have always made the book immensely popular in schools across the country often torn asunder by the same kinds of cliques described in the story.
The cast has tremendous energy and performs the show with celerity and passionate verve. But the performances are very rough due to the limited experience of some of the performers. At times, the actors seem to be speaking lines and making gestures in obvious performance rather than being the characters in a natural way that is more fluid than stiff, more polished than stilted.
Though the rough veneer of some performances in a way mirrors the rough and tumble world of the show, there are stand outs. Chief of these is Nick Wheeler, last seen in “Peter and the Starcatcher.” Wheeler is a natural actor and has the perfect look to be Ponyboy. He’s also the glue that bonds this show together in a way that is both essential and beautiful.
After many small roles over the last few years at WAD, Christian Perez pulls out a plum as Dallas Winston, an older Greaser and ex-con. His big body is perfect for the character, and Perez shows talents playing a character much different than those he’s played before.
Hunter King also continues to impress in the roles he plays, though his first act work is at times a bit too overwrought and far too trembly. However, King makes up for this in the second act with some very natural work, showing why he is such a fine and promising actor.
The cast as a whole supports these three main characters well, and though rough at times, the awkward line deliveries and inconsistencies are short-lived and brief in this fast-paced show which clocks in at well under two hours.
As always, director Randy Wolf has a keen eye and ear for the mood he wishes to set and has a smart crew of designers and technical folk to bring his vision to life. Music is used especially well in this production, including a choice bit that really sets the tone from Joni Mitchell’s live album “Shadows and Light.” Scrim work of shadows and light presents silhouettes of characters throughout the show, reinforcing this idea of light and dark in another way.
Though perhaps best to avoid the depiction of what has brought this book under fire, the lack of smoking and drinking in the show is probably the wrong choice and does not best serve the overarching message of the realities of “juvenile delinquents,” the term for at-risk-youth in the era that “The Outsiders” was written.
Sets by Samantha Snow are simple but utilitarian and appropriate for the story, featuring two large chain link fence pieces that remind viewers throughout the show of the cage in which the characters find themselves.
What A Do continues to show local audiences it knows what to do with drama. And though as Robert Frost’s poem says (which is quoted in the show) that “nothing gold can stay,” this gold will be staying through two more weeks of performances.
WHEN: 7:30 p.m. Feb. 16-17, 24-25; 3 p.m. Feb. 18 and 26.
WHERE: 4071 W. Dickman Road, Springfield.
COST: $20 general admission; $15 student, senior and military; pay what you can on Feb. 16.

User: How did the Greek philosophy of stoicism impact Roman art?
Agent: The philosophy of stoicism, which emphasized self-control, rationality, and acceptance of one's fate, had a significant impact on Roman art. Stoicism was popularized by the Roman philosopher Seneca, who stressed the importance of moral virtue and living in harmony with nature. Roman artists sought to express these ideals in their works, using stoic themes and motifs to convey a sense of order, stability, and rationality.

Stoicism was particularly influential in Roman sculpture, where artists often depicted heroic figures embodying stoic virtues such as courage, discipline, and endurance. These figures, such as Marcus Aurelius on horseback or the Roman emperor Augustus, were often shown in a pose of calm authority, emphasizing their control over their own destiny.

Stoicism also influenced Roman architecture, as seen in the use of simple geometric forms, clean lines, and restrained ornamentation in buildings such as the Pantheon and the Forum. These structures were designed to convey a sense of grandeur and permanence, reflecting the stoic ideals of rationality, order, and enduring virtue.

Overall, the stoic philosophy played a significant role in shaping Roman art, providing artists with a set of values and ideals that they could use to create works of enduring beauty and meaning.

An ordinance passed in 2010, said dogs could bark for up to 20 consecutive minutes before a neighbor could issue a complaint. That was revised recently so that neighbors can file a complaint if a dog is making excessive noise for 10 minutes during the day and only five minutes at night.
Owners are then issued a written warning and are given five days -- instead of seven like in 2010 -- to find a solution to the problem.
If an owner fails to remedy the situation within the five day time period, the consequences can make them howl. Pet owners face a $50 fine for the first offense and $75 for the second. If the problem persists, the pet owner is subject to automatic summons and a judge determines the severity of the fine.
Many owners choose to seek help rather than face fines.

Liebowitz says a barking dog is normally an unhappy dog, so treating it may not be as simple as training your dog to stop barking on command.
"Barking is usually a symptom of a dog who is not fulfilled. They're trying to communicate that. It's often separation anxiety...Maybe 25 percent of our business comes from dog owners who are gone during the day."
Liebowitz says evolving training, along with changes in the way people view their dogs, is the solution to the barking conundrum.
"Ten years ago, when a dog was barking, they'd just put a shock collar on it and shut it up. I think they're more attune to the fact that dogs have needs," he said.
Liebowitz has several suggestions to ease a lonely pet's mind. If a dog is barking because of social isolation, he suggests increasing its "people time" by going for walks.
Liebowitz recommends increasing the use of chew toys and exercise. However, if barking persists, he suggests consulting a vet, as medication may be required for extreme cases of separation anxiety.
Liebowitz's company offers several options for training, but he says the most popular are the in-home private consultation sessions costing $150 a pop.
Liebowitz says there are more complaints about barking dogs because more people are getting dogs.
Liam Crowe, CEO of Barkbusters USA, has also seen an increase in business and he says it's not just the number of dogs that is increasing.
"I think peoples' tolerance level has been tested over the last few years. Dogs are becoming more popular. They're one of the fastest growing industries in the country," Crowe said. "A lot of people are putting off having children until they're older, so they get a dog instead."
"We provide people with a solution to barking. Regardless of the changing laws, it's very simple to instill," Crowe said. "A happy dog doesn't sit there and bark all day. Once we take that stress away from a dog, you can almost see the smile on their face."

User: Provide step-by-step instructions on the process of training a dog to sit, stay, and come when called using positive reinforcement techniques. Include tips on how to handle common issues when training, such as distractions, reluctance, or disobedience, and suggest ways to modify the training according to the dog's temperament and age. Provide examples of successful training sessions and describe how to gradually increase the difficulty and variety of the exercises while keeping the dog engaged and motivated. Emphasize the importance of consistency, patience, and praise in building a strong relationship between the owner and the dog through training.
Agent: Training a dog to sit, stay, and come when called using positive reinforcement techniques can be rewarding for both the dog and the owner. Here are the step-by-step instructions for the training process:

1. Choose a quiet and comfortable training location. It should be free of distractions, like toys or other animals, where the dog can focus on the training.

2. Have a treat or a favorite toy ready. Positive reinforcement is an effective technique, which means rewarding your dog for doing the right thing with treats and praise.

3. Start by teaching your dog to sit. Hold a treat close to the dog's nose, and slowly move your hand upwards towards their eyes. The dog should follow the treat with their eyes, causing their head to tilt up, and their butt to lower down. Once the dog is in the sitting position, say "Sit" and offer the treat or toy as a reward.

4. Once the dog is responding to the "Sit" command consistently, move on to the "Stay" command. Ask your dog to sit, and then put your hand out in front of their face, saying "Stay" in a firm tone. Take a step backward, and if the dog stays put, reward them with a treat or toy. Gradually increase the distance between you and the dog, but return quickly to the dog and reward them consistently.

5. To train your dog to come when called, start by attaching a long lead to their collar. Walk a few steps away from the dog and say "Come" in a friendly tone, immediately patting your knee to encourage the dog to come to you. Once they do, reward them with a treat or toy. Gradually increase the distance you call them from, and the time you ask them to stay before coming.

Tips:

- Use a high-pitched, cheerful tone when rewarding your dog to indicate that they did the right thing
- If the dog seems reluctant or disobedient, try breaking the training session into shorter intervals or changing the treats or toys you use as rewards
- For distractions, like other dogs or people, practice training in gradually more crowded areas
- Adjust the training pace according to the dog's age, temperament, and skill level, and do not overwork them
- To keep your dog engaged and motivated, create a positive and loving atmosphere during training, and counteract boredom by adding variety to the exercises
- Consistency is key. Be patient and keep up a regular training schedule. Praising good behavior and using consistent commands helps to build a bond between the owner and the dog.

Example of a training session:

In the first session, the owner of the dog called Tony takes him to a quiet park. He has a bag of treats and a toy ready. He starts by teaching Tony to sit by holding the treat close to Tony's nose, moving his hand up and saying "Sit". When Tony does it correctly, he praises him and gives him a treat.

Next, he asks Tony to sit, and then adds the "Stay" command, stepping back while saying "Stay". Tony gets up to follow, but the owner uses his firm voice to stop him, and he manages to stay while the owner takes a few steps back. When the owner returns, he rewards Tony with a treat.

Finally, the owner attaches a long lead to Tony's collar, and walks a few steps away. He calls Tony in a friendly tone, patting his knee, and Tony comes quickly. Once again, the owner rewards him with a treat.

For the next session, the owner increases the distance for "Stay" and "Come" commands.

Gradually increasing the difficulty and variety of exercises:

As Tony gets better at sitting, staying, and coming, the owner can add distractions and more complex exercises. For example, he can ask Tony to sit and stay while he walks around him, or while throwing a ball. The owner can also try varying the length of time he asks Tony to stay, or changing the vocal cues for each command. By keeping Tony engaged and motivated, the owner helps him to get better at these commands, which boosts his confidence and strengthens their bond.

User: Write a tutorial on how to train a dog to respond to basic commands.
Agent: Training a dog to respond to basic commands can be a fun and rewarding process for both you and your furry friend. Here is a step-by-step tutorial on how to train a dog to respond to basic commands.

Step 1: Choose your command words
Decide on the words you will use for your commands, such as "sit", "stay", "come", "heel" and "down". Use consistent command words for each action so your dog can easily learn and remember them.

Step 2: Begin with basic commands
Start with basic commands such as "sit" and "come" before moving on to more complicated commands.

Step 3: Use positive reinforcement
Positive reinforcement is key to training your dog to respond to commands. Reward your dog with praise, petting, and/or treats when they respond correctly to your commands.

Step 4: Keep training sessions short
Dogs have short attention spans so keep training sessions short, about 10-15 minutes each time. Make training a daily routine to help your dog remember the commands.

Step 5: Teaching "sit"
Begin with the "sit" command. Hold a treat near your dog's nose and slowly move it upward. Your dog's head should follow the treat, causing their bottom to lower. When their bottom touches the ground, say "sit" and give them the treat. Repeat this several times until they're following the command without the treat.

Step 6: Teaching "come"
The "come" command is important for calling your dog to you. When your dog is nearby, say "come" in a positive tone and reward them once they reach you. Repeat this, gradually increasing the distance between you and your dog.

Step 7: Teaching "stay"
With your dog in the "sit" position, give the "stay" command and move a bit back from your dog. If your dog stays in the position, reward them. Gradually increase your distance, but be ready to guide your dog from afar if they begin to stray.

Step 8: Teaching "heel" and "down"
The "heel" command teaches your dog to walk calmly by your side while the "down" command teaches them to lie down on command.

Step 9: Practice regularly
Practice regularly to improve your dog's responsiveness to commands. Reinforce commands with treats, praise, and petting.

Step 10: Stay Patient and Consistent
Training your dog requires patience and consistency. Don't get frustrated if your dog doesn't respond immediately. Consistency is key. With enough practice, your dog will eventually learn to respond to your commands. 

Remember, training your dog is a process, and it requires time and patience, but it will definitely pay off in the end. Happy training!
